# Introduction

In `ESS11e04_2/ESS11e04_2.csv` you can find a (large) dataset from a social study 
conducted throughout the EU. More information can be found [here](https://ess.sikt.no/en/datafile/242aaa39-3bbb-40f5-98bf-bfb1ce53d8ef?tab=0&elems=4cfef379-934d-41e6-8c3c-4b77f9d91232). You can also find more on the variables,
and many descriptive statistics in `ESS11e04_2 codebook.html` (open in any browser).

We are going to work with those data to showcase some (mostly) descriptive 
statistics manipulations using R.

## Simple Hypothesis Testing

First, reload the dataset:

```{r}
ess_pol <- read.csv('ess_pol.csv', sep = ',')
summary(ess_pol)
```
Let us also review the aggregate distribution of all those variables per country:

```{r}
aggregate(ess_pol, by = list(ess_pol$ess_data.cntry), FUN = mean)

```

The wrong way to proceed at this stage is to use a t-test to compare, say, Austria with Belgium, in terms of time devoted into politics related news:

```{r}
# THIS IS WRONG!
austria <- ess_pol[ess_pol$ess_data.cntry == 'AT', ]
belgium <- ess_pol[ess_pol$ess_data.cntry == 'BE', ]
t.test(austria$ess_data.nwspol, belgium$ess_nwspol)
```

The first error here is that we have not cleaned our data, i.e., we have not dropped any dummy values. For example, as one reads [here](ESS11e04_2 codebook.html), 9999 for example, in `nwspol` means that no answer was provided, while 8888 and 7777 also have a meaning. So, one first approach might be:

```{r}
austria <- austria[!(austria$ess_data.nwspol %in% c(7777,8888,9999)) , ]
summary(austria)
```

Now we observe that there is at least one participant that devotes 1200 minutes (20 hours) per day on politics news. Since this might be a mistyped value, we might impose a seemingly artificial but, more or less, sound limit, e.g., by filtering out extreme values, too.

In our case, we first examine how many such extremities occur:

```{r}
length(austria[austria$ess_data.nwspol > 600, ])
```

Since there are not that many extreme values, our choice does not make any substantial difference, so we might decide to keep those observations too. We now proceed to clean Belgium data too:

```{r}
belgium <- belgium[!(belgium$ess_data.nwspol %in% c(7777,8888,9999)) , ]
summary(belgium)
```
Let us again count extreme values:

```{r}
length(belgium[belgium$ess_data.nwspol > 600, ])
```


Again, we keep those as well. In case the extreme values for Belgians were far too many, we might have needed to revise our choice for Austria, too.

Now, we feel (are we?) ready to perform a better t-test:

```{r}
t.test(austria$ess_data.nwspol, belgium$ess_data.nwspol)
```

So, again, we get the same result with quite a lot of confidence ($p<10^{-15}$),
that is, the probability of Type I error is:

$$p<0.000000000000001$$
Again, are we allowed to use a t-test here? To use a t-test, we assume:

* at first, that both populations are normally distributed, and;
* no knowledge of population SD.

The second hypothesis if fulfilled but what about the first one?

The first step might be to plot the actual distribution, i.e., a histogram:

```{r}
hist(austria$ess_data.nwspol)
```

This is a bad histogram for many reasons, the most obvious being that we have too few bins (most of those being empty). We can make two (at least) changes to make things better:

* use more bins;
* exclude (temprorarily) any outliers.

```{r}
austria_hist <- austria[austria$ess_data.nwspol < 600, ]
hist(austria_hist$ess_data.nwspol, breaks=50)
```

So, we can evidently infer that the distribution of our sample is not normal so, we should not have used the t-test in our case. We will explore in the future more adequate tests for populations of unknown distribution.

> As a side note, a better histogram would have included all outliers in a separate unevenly sized bin:

```{r}
hist(austria$ess_data.nwspol, breaks=c(seq(0, 200, 10), 1200))
```
